title: Technology and the Future Workforce in the US

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Work isn’t that it used to be, and in the future it won’t be what it is now. Standardization, mechanization, electrification, and more recently robotification and computerization have driven constant change for more than a century. The changes have been disruptive for many workers as jobs have disappeared, and many communities have suffered long-term decline when their dominant industries withered. In the long run, however, technological progress has been beneficial. As some joins have been made obsolete, new ones have been created, the economy has adjusted, and society has been better off.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: But things may be different this time. In earlier time, the transformation of agriculture occurred across a great span of time, giving social systems a longer opportunity to adjust. Now, as the rate of technological advancement is rapidly accelerating, one can only hope that our social systems can become increasingly efficient. If not, the next stage in the evolution of work might prove disastrous for the displaced workers. It seems certain that technological progress will make the economy stronger, but some question its ability to lift all workers and enhance economic equity, while others debate the pace of change.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: We might find it difficult to provide education that supports not just the privileged, hut all members of society. Will traditional and short-term degrees still be able to guarantee a middle class lifestyle? Or will governments have to provide financial backing for ever-more advanced and complex job training, so that workers can keep up with the changes in technology? These are issues on which many scholars have presented differing perspectives.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: French economist Thomas Piketty looks at the interplay of technological change and larger economic trends in Capital in the 21st Century. He sees advances in technology and the opportunities they provide as forces for social equity. However, he worries that these advances are too weak to offset deeper changes in the structure of the economy, leading to greater concentration of wealth and income for just a few. The labor economist David Autor, of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), thinks that most commentators exaggerate the competition that robots computers present, and in turn, play down the importance of the unspoken knowledge and integrated skills that people possess. He acknowledges that machines are ideal for ordinary tasks, but he finds that most jobs entail specialized tasks at which humans are superior. He expects workers to enhance their productivity and value by enlisting machines of various types to perform the easy, routine aspects of their jobs, giving them more time to complete the non-routine tasks.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: Harvard University economist and former treasury secretary Lawrence Summers looks at ongoing changes in the labor market as a sign that trouble is already here. He says that, as a student, he learned and accepted the cheerful view that technology would boost productivity and ultimately benefit workers. But he found it easier to accept that view when the unemployment rate of US males between the ages of 25 and 54 was low, at 6%. At more than double that level and likely to persist, Summers observes that this factor significantly changes the ability of workers to bargain with their employers, and reduces the likelihood that this large group of workers will so their earnings increase. He also asks what makes US productivity growth so sluggish, in spite of this so-called revolution in workplace technology.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: A more optimistic view comes from Thomas H Davenport and Julia Kirby in their article ‘Beyond Automation’ in Harvard Business Review. Davenport and Kirby follow David Autor’s line of thinking in arguing that technology only enhances human labor, and they develop a variety of strategies by which people can position themselves to benefit from ever more sophisticated mechanization. Unfortunately, the examples they provide refer largely to the highly skilled and educated workers in the top 20% of the wage distribution.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: The effects of change will differ among industries, across the nature and level of skill, and among demographic groups. Scholar Mark Schneider, for example, explores the changing world of credentials that are becoming alternatives to the typical college experience which takes place over four to eight years. A one-year certificate in a technical field may replace a traditional four-year degree as a sound foundation for a successful career, and the government might step in to support the more extensive and particular educational agendas likely to be in demand.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Economics Professor Donna Gintherz examines those at the top rung of the education ladder: PhDs in engineering and the fields of physical, life, and social sciences. Their futures have long been quite predictable, but now they are likely to experience some disruption. While an advanced degree was once a fairly reliable guarantee of employment in an academic field, the computerdriven changes in the landscape of higher education have blurred the definition of expertise. There are no longer guarantees. Technology is changing the educational order Although the pessimists and optimists disagree on how well society will adjust to technologydriven changes in the workplace, they all agree that change is coming and adaptation will be needed.

groups.title: Technological Progress
content: For more than one century, technological innovation such as mechanisation and electrification has continually created major changes for the workforce and weakened a lot of communities for long periods. However, it has also made the economy more productive. While some kinds of work became {{23}} , others emerged and eventually created stability, sometimes offering better conditions in the long run. In previous centuries, changes in {{24}} had taken place over a much longer time, and societies had time to adapt. Now, technological improvements are occurring at such a rapid pace that social structures must also become more {{25}} . Experts have studied different aspects of this problem, such as whether education will only benefit the rich. and whether money from {{26}} will have to support more specialised careers.
